extracted.intended_audience: schools and recipients of Federal education funding (Title IX coordinators, school administrators, legal counsel), plus policymakers and commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble to final Title IX regulations explaining what conduct and protected traits constitute sex discrimination (e.g., sexual orientation, sex characteristics, sex stereotypes, pregnancy, menstruation), how harm is assessed (de minimis harm standard), and related recipient obligations (privacy, training, reasonable modifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual orientation is prohibited sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation under Title IX (see §106.10). A recipient's intentional separation or different treatment of students based on their sexual orientation generally would constitute sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the regulations permit separation on the basis of “sex,” §106.10 does not permit a recipient to separate students on the basis of sexual orientation or other bases in §106.10 (such as pregnancy or sex stereotypes). Nothing in these final regulations impacts any private associational rights of lesbian, gay, and bisexual individuals. Cites Bostock, 590 U.S. at 659-62.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on discrimination based on sex characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.10 prohibits discrimination based on sex characteristics, intended to refer to physiological sex-based characteristics (including anatomy, hormones, and chromosomes associated with male or female bodies); discrimination based on intersex traits is included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discrimination based on a person's physiological sex characteristics could be considered sex discrimination regardless of any specific medical diagnosis and is not limited to reproductive capacity. Examples the Department recognizes (but declines to definitively catalogue due to fact-specific analysis) include inappropriate disclosure of medical information about a student's intersex traits or denial of access to sex-separate facilities consistent with a student's gender identity based on intersex traits. The Department uses the more accessible term 'intersex' while acknowledging related clinical terminology (e.g., differences of sex development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex stereotyping as a form of sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex stereotypes—described as 'fixed or generalized expectations regarding a person's aptitudes, behavior, self-presentation, or other attributes based on sex'—can constitute sex discrimination when they operate to exclude a person from participation in, deny benefits of, or otherwise subject a person to discrimination under a recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all conduct one might label 'sex stereotyping' necessarily violates Title IX. To establish sex discrimination based on sex stereotypes, the policy, practice, or conduct must, on the basis of sex, exclude, deny benefits, or otherwise subject a person to discrimination. Courts have applied Price Waterhouse reasoning in this context (e.g., Whitaker, Pederson). The Department also clarifies that application of sex-specific rules/practices is not automatically sex stereotyping. See §106.31(a)(2) regarding permissible sex separation carried out without imposing more than de minimis harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pregnancy or related conditions are protected
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.10 makes clear that Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination includes discrimination based on pregnancy or related conditions; harassment based on pregnancy or related conditions is a form of sex-based harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes that Title IX regulations (and prior versions) have long prohibited pregnancy discrimination and that the final regulations clarify and extend protections across a recipient's education program or activity. The Department declines to add 'current, potential, or past' to §106.10 because §§106.21(c), 106.40(b)(1), and 106.57(b) already prohibit discrimination based on 'current, potential, or past pregnancy or related conditions.' The meaning of 'related conditions' is defined in §106.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Menstruation and related conditions fall within sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrimination based on menstruation, perimenopause, menopause, or related conditions is sex discrimination because it can overlap or fall within pregnancy/related conditions, sex stereotypes, or sex characteristics under §106.10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Menstruation, perimenopause, and menopause (and associated medical conditions) can create barriers to participation; examples include unnecessary bathroom restrictions, discipline for bleeding, harassment, or requirements that publicly expose that a student is menstruating. The Department concluded explicit regulatory text was unnecessary because such discrimination is already covered. The Department declines to mandate reasonable modifications or provision of menstrual products but notes recipients may provide those, and that many menstruation-related issues can be addressed through compliance with §106.10. If a condition meets the definition of 'pregnancy or related conditions' (§106.2) or qualifies as a disability under Section 504/the ADA, different or additional obligations (e.g., reasonable modifications) may apply (§106.40(b)(3)(ii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy limits on menstruation-related records and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients should not collect or maintain more information than necessary about menstruation-related records; personally identifiable information obtained in the course of complying with this part must not be disclosed except in limited circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised §106.44(j) to prohibit recipients from disclosing personally identifiable information obtained under these regulations, with limited exceptions. The Department emphasizes privacy concerns about tracking menstrual cycles or sharing menstruation-related data with law enforcement, and will offer technical assistance to promote compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training obligations for staff on scope of sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §106.8(d)(1), all employees must be trained on the recipient's obligation to address sex discrimination and the scope of conduct that constitutes sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to mandate training content beyond that general requirement, allowing recipients flexibility in content. Because discrimination based on menstruation or related conditions falls within §106.10, recipients may benefit from including such topics in trainings for Title IX Coordinators and staff. The Department may consider issuing future guidance and technical assistance with examples and sample survey questions but does not require menstrual education for students (the Department does not control school curricula per 20 U.S.C. 1232a).

rubrics_metrics.name: De minimis harm standard for permissible sex separation (§106.31(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department explains that sex-based separation or different treatment is presumptively discriminatory, but limited contexts permit separation where it does not subject a person to more than de minimis harm; a recipient must not provide sex-separate facilities or activities in a manner that subjects any person to legally cognizable injury (i.e., more than de minimis harm) unless a statutory basis allows otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The de minimis harm standard is grounded in case law recognizing that discrimination includes an element of injury or harm (e.g., Oncale, Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co., Bostock). The regulation seeks to explain legal authority for permitting sex separation in certain circumstances and the limitations on how recipients may carry out separation. The Department rejects claims the standard is inconsistent with Title IX or hostile-environment law and rejects arguments invoking the major questions doctrine regarding §§106.10 and 106.31(a)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective, reasonable-person assessment of harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Harm under §106.31(a)(2) must be genuine and objectively non-trivial and assessed from the perspective of a reasonable person in the individual's position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department clarifies that the inquiry is objective and judicially administrable, avoiding reliance on a plaintiff's unusual subjective feelings (citing Burlington). Injuries, including stigmatic injuries associated with differential treatment on the basis of sex, can satisfy the standard without requiring an additional showing of more 'material' harm. The Department notes examples of relevant case law and that assessing harm objectively is consistent with longstanding anti-discrimination law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient duty to address barriers and remedy effects (§106.44)
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent discrimination (including menstruation-related discrimination) becomes a barrier to participation in a recipient's education program or activity, schools have an obligation to address such barriers, prevent recurrence, and remedy their effects per §106.44(a) and (f)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of barriers include menstruation-related harassment, unreasonable limits on bathroom access, conduct by school officials that publicly exposes a student's menstruation (e.g., requiring removal of a garment), or similar restrictions or discipline. The Department expects recipients to address these barriers through complaint processes and corrective actions described in §106.44.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable modifications for menstruation not mandated but available
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to require recipients to provide reasonable modifications specifically for menstruation or to require access to menstrual products, but nothing precludes recipients from using discretion to provide such modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will continue to study whether further action is needed. Many menstruation-related issues will be addressed by compliance with §106.10 (e.g., flexible dress codes, addressing harassment). If a menstruation-related condition meets the definition of 'pregnancy or related conditions' (§106.2), a student is entitled to reasonable modifications under §106.40(b)(3)(ii). If it qualifies as a disability under Section 504 or the ADA, the individual must be provided full rights under those laws, including reasonable modifications.
